en: Seeing him, I took fright.
Akbaltay's lion,
Escaping, brought word;
To Bakay and the lion Manas
That Chubak had gone.
“Hero Manas, hear my grievance:
In Bukhara, that great city,
When I sought to seize its khanship,
What turmoil I encountered!
Tearing my nine coats,
Of middle height and broad shoulders,
Having received a written letter from the caliph,
Known as a blood-drinker,
Holding a blue Zulpukor spear,
With a naked sword bound at the side,
Riding a black, white-blazed horse,
Its hairy tail tied tight,
Coming out across my path to fight,
We fought many spear bouts.
I made that foe thrust many spears;
Of all those swords and spears,
I broke them without leaving one.
That one exhausted
My beast, Kokala.
I never saw such a fierce warrior.
Khan Manas, had you not been here,
That foe would have spilled my blood,
Pursuing cruelly without turning back,
Draining my strength.
Thrusting four times for my one,
That foe disgraced me terribly.
I have lost faith in the Oygut;
No companion came behind me.
This year I shall move to Talas,
And come to serve as a warrior
To famous Sultan Manas.
Bringing my household to Keng-Kol,
From stately Bukhara,
If I live, I shall exact
Revenge for what I have suffered.”
“Akbaltay's lion,
Your words are truly right;
There is no twisting or evasion,
What you have said is wholly true.
This world is fleeting, only two days;
Be friends into the next world.
So that you never part,
Chew white wheat flour together.
My son, I am Lion Bakay;
Let me tell you the truth.
To bring slaughter upon the emperor,
To take revenge upon the unbelievers,
To bring slaughter upon Beijing,
To destroy them utterly,
Chew white wheat flour.
My son, hold to the sacred oath.
Come and settle in Talas,
Come and serve as a warrior
To Manas, Jakyp's only son.
If you come and settle in Talas,
That is the place to dispel your sorrow;
He is the hero who will tend you without grief.
My son, come to Manas and you will prosper;
You will thrive, playing the knucklebone game.
My son, I am Oluyat's son;
My son, you are Khan Baltay's son.
I grew up and girded my waist.
At the world's end lies Zhelpinish;
In that Zhelpinish I was born.
At only six I grew restless;
When I reached seven years,
I saw Manas in a dream;
Now I have met Khan Manas.
At the world's end, in Zhelpinish,
Before Manas was born,
I sought him for seven years.
In the cities of Baghdad and Egypt,
I searched for six years.
In Mecca and Medina,
For five years I could not find him.
Yesterday, when God granted my wish,
When I reached thirty-one,
Finding no land like Talas,
Finding no hero like Khan Manas,
My courage made me restless, Chubak.
On Andijan's gray plain, Chubak,
I met Lion Khan Manas.
Sleeping at noon, I heard word
That Khan Akbaltay's lion
To generous, fierce Manas
Would become a sworn warrior.
My companion in death, my partner in life,
We rode ahead toward Andijan.
To find you, my precious one,
We waited, looking toward Andijan.
I was a holy sage myself, Chubak,
I was Khan Bakay's eye.
To go and settle in Talas,
To become Manas's warrior,
You were wandering astray, Chubak.
Seeking you deliberately, making a path,
Your village was among the Oygut.
News of you came from Bukhara.
Dueling with a woman,
Chubak, this was your disgrace.
Well, that person from Bukhara whom you fought—
She is the wife Khan Manas will take.
A beauty among the dark-complexioned,
She is radiant among Muslims.
The most capable of women,
A saint among women,
A woman of extraordinary strength,
A treasure for Khan Manas.
Often, Chubak, you will know:
By your excellent, ill-fated sister-in-law,
Chubak, you will wear the coat she makes.
Chubak, on your right are Russians;
Chubak, beyond the ridge are Chinese.
Chubak, before you are Franks.
If sovereign Khan Manas lives and thrives,
You have many enemies to fight.
If God grants it, my Chubak,
Your time will come to be a sultan.
Kanykey, Khan Temir's daughter—
Chubak, do not grieve;
This year she is to become your sister-in-law.
This year, Chubak, hear my words:
This year we shall range through Medina.
For Manas, visited by Kyzyr,
We shall find valiant men.
For Manas, visited by Baabedin,
We shall find many heroes.
On the ridge of Kum-Bulak,
On the journey to Mecca,
At the place of ritual washing,
One champion among fanged creatures
Will meet the generous khan.
If it lives, a gray puppy
Will be found for Khan Manas.
We shall take Kumayyk along the way.
To tend Kumayyk,
Using that as a pretext,
Putting betrothal earrings on that poor woman,
We shall take Kanykey as bride.
She is the support to rely upon;
Born of a woman,
She is that exceptionally strong hero.
As queen to the blood-stained warrior,
She is the one who will find a way for us.”
Acting as mediator, Khan Bakay
Spoke words of prophecy.
Speaking words full of meaning,
Proclaiming all that was to be said,
Comforting Khan Chubak,
He returned to Talas.
He made the meaning known
To your royal father Manas.
Khan Bakay, born a leopard,
Spoke words of sacred power.
Resourceful Bakay, that holy elder,
Persuading Chubak skillfully,
Took him to Talas then.
Chubak went and settled in Talas;
He became your father Sultan Manas's warrior.
Ajybay, Khan Argyn's son,
Rode to Talas,
And then became a warrior
To your father Sultan Manas.
Your father gathered heroes through his valor.
He gathered twelve generations alike.
The horses grew fat and strong.
Through his greatness of spirit, your father
Alone was worth forty men.
Fortune favored him in everything;
He was a lion favored with victory.
The one God, someone like your father,
A soul created to equal your father,
Will not grant again soon.
Your father made trouble wherever he sought;
Using Kumayyk as a pretext,
Loading eighty camels with gold coins,
He made a marriage alliance and took me.
He showed me many humiliations,
Stirring quarrels time and again;
Your father subjected me to much oppression.
Your father Manas, looming large,
When he came to court me,
My father was beside himself with joy,
And gathered holy men, leaving none out.
Seventy mullahs and four scholars
Joined your fierce father Khan Manas
In marriage to your wretched mother.
Ninety young wives and ninety girls
Laid bedding without pause,
Taking gold by the pood, countless gold coins,
As gifts for the bride's womenfolk.
To lie in his embrace,
When I, wretched one, stepped forward,
Just as I reached the bed,
My steel blade on the lattice wall
Leapt from its sheath,
And your father, visited by Kyzyr,
It lightly scratched across the forearm.
Putting sorrow upon me,
Saying, “As a girl, this bitch
Stabbed and wounded my forearm,”
He left without lying in my embrace.
I acquired an ill name,
Your khan father would not sleep with me;
Again I became a neglected wife.
Struggling, he won his prize;
Using that as a pretext, your father
Bukhara, where my father Khan Temir lived,
He raided six times.
For Akbaltay's Chubak,
That unruly one who had fought me,
He attacked the moving camps at will,
And thus took his revenge.
I was the one left neglected.
Bearing your father no resentment,
With sixty girls and their white yurts,
I came out of Bukhara,
And settled beside your father.
Finding my way, with your father
Winning favor through my skill,
At long last I became his wife, my son!
Go safely and return safely, my son;
Against Abyke and Kobosh,
Do not wage a shooting war and slaughter!
Let me name the time:
My foal, return within sixty days.
Take Buurul and make him a fine courser.
My orphan who will ease my sorrow,
Make those six villains your kin.”
His mother Kanykey, gathering force,
Finished telling her tale,
Burning orphan Semetey's heart.
From those dear eyes like a quail's,
Tears fell one after another.
From those dear eyes like currants,
Saying, “My beloved orphan son,”
Tears flowed a whip-length long.
“That dear bird called the wild duck
Flies without turning back, for the open plain.
How much I have suffered, wretched soul,
For the child who came from my womb.
My river and spring with their valley,
My unruly boy, whom I gained at long last,
Go to your six uncles and return.
If they give you your property,
Take it without causing distress.
If they do not give it, my foal,
Return without trading insults.
Saying, 'Mother, they would not give it,'
Come and tell me, wretched woman.
My son, if you wreak havoc, it brings an ill name.
